title: eBay, the online auction site, goes public
what: eBay of San Jose sold 3.5 million shares on the Nasdaq at $18 each; on the first day they closed at about $53, valuing the company at nearly $1.9 billion. eBay runs a website where people auction goods to each other, from Beanie Babies to collectibles, and takes a fee on each sale. It had more than 1 million registered users at the end of August and, unlike most internet companies, it makes a profit.
why: The listing beat (importance 1). The case for buying: a marketplace that holds no stock, ships nothing and is profitable; the shares rose 839% in their first year.

title: eBay raises $700 million at $170 a share
what: eBay sold 4.25 million new shares at $170 each, raising about $696 million. Its online revenue grew 74% in the first quarter over the previous quarter. Its registered users passed 2.1 million at the end of 1998, when revenue for the year reached $47 million.
why: eBay uses its sky-high share price to raise cash; the shares rose 52% in April 1999, the top of the first eBay bubble.

title: eBay's website goes down for nearly a day
what: eBay's website suffered a major outage on June 10, halting auctions across the site. The company is crediting users $3.9 million in fees and has started a full review of its systems.
why: The outage exposed how fragile the fast-growing dot-coms' technology was and hit eBay's growth for the quarter.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065088/0001012870-99-002671.txt (10-Q for the quarter to June 30, 1999, read 2026-10-03)

title: eBay's growth slows after the outage
what: eBay's online revenue grew only 12% in the second quarter over the first, or 27% without the outage credits, after 74% the quarter before. Total revenue was $49.5 million, against $19.5 million a year earlier.
why: Slower growth and a sell-off in internet shares: eBay fell 35% in July 1999. The figures are from the quarterly filing (filed August 9); the date of the July earnings release was not confirmed.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065088/0001012870-99-002671.txt (10-Q for the quarter to June 30, 1999, read 2026-10-03)

title: eBay doubles revenue and stays profitable
what: eBay's revenue for 2000 rose to $431 million from $225 million and net income to $48 million. It has 22.5 million registered users. In January it agreed to buy a majority of Internet Auction, the leading auction site in South Korea, and announced higher fees in the United States from January 31.
why: The rare dot-com that kept growing and earning through the crash; the shares rebounded 50% in January 2001 after falling a third in November. The annual figures are from the 10-K; the date of the January earnings release was not confirmed.

title: eBay's revenue up 79%
what: eBay's revenue for the first quarter rose 79% to $154 million from $86 million a year earlier, helped by more users and listings and by the fee increases of January 31.
why: eBay is one of the few internet stocks to recover in 2001; +39% in April, +20% in May.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065088/000109581101502243/f72456e10-q.txt (10-Q for the quarter to March 31, 2001, read 2026-10-03)

title: eBay completes its purchase of PayPal
what: eBay completed its acquisition of PayPal, an online payment service widely used by eBay buyers, for $1.4 billion on October 3. It will phase out its own payment service, Billpoint.
why: The most important deal in eBay's history: PayPal became eBay's second pillar and was spun off in 2015.

title: eBay raises its forecast to $3 billion
what: eBay reported record fourth-quarter revenue of $648 million, up 57%, and 2003 revenue of $2.17 billion, up 78%, with net income of $442 million. It raised its 2004 revenue forecast to $3 billion.
why: eBay at full speed, with PayPal growing inside it; the shares peaked as a growth stock in December 2004.

title: eBay's record quarter disappoints
what: On January 19 eBay reported record fourth-quarter revenue of $935.8 million, up 44%, and 2004 revenue of $3.27 billion, up 51%, with net income of $778 million, and announced a two-for-one share split. But its forecast of $1.01 billion to $1.03 billion revenue for the first quarter of 2005 implies much slower growth.
why: The peak of eBay as a growth stock: the shares fell 30% in January 2005 and kept falling for four years (-81% to 2009-02).

title: eBay buys Skype for $2.6 billion
what: eBay has acquired Skype, which offers free telephone calls over the internet, for $2.6 billion. eBay plans to tie it into its marketplace.
why: An expensive misfit: eBay sold 70% of Skype in 2009 and Microsoft later bought it for $8.5 billion.

title: eBay's revenue grows 30% but the stock slumps
what: eBay reported record second-quarter revenue of $1.41 billion, up 30%, with growth from the marketplaces, PayPal and Skype, and announced a $2 billion share buyback. About 35% of the goods sold on eBay now sell at fixed prices.
why: The shares fell 18% in July 2006, the low of the 2005-06 slide (cause of the reaction not confirmed in the sources read).

title: Meg Whitman steps down at eBay
what: Meg Whitman, who has run eBay since 1998 when it had 30 employees, resigned as chief executive and was replaced by John Donahoe. Whitman remains on the board.
why: The end of the founding era; the shares fell 19% in January 2008.

title: eBay buys GSI Commerce
what: eBay acquired GSI Commerce, which runs online shops for large retailers, for $2.4 billion.
why: Part of Donahoe's attempt to turn eBay into a commerce-technology company; the business was renamed eBay Enterprise in 2013.

title: eBay's revenue tops $14 billion
what: eBay reported 2012 revenue of $14.1 billion, up 21%. Chief executive John Donahoe said the company had a great finish to the year; fixed-price sales on the marketplace grew 21%.
why: The Donahoe turnaround at its best; the shares rose about two thirds in 2012.

title: eBay to spin off PayPal
what: On September 30 eBay announced it will separate PayPal into an independent listed company, as the activist investor Carl Icahn demanded at the start of the year.
why: The break-up of eBay; holders kept both companies.

title: PayPal becomes a separate company
what: eBay completed the spin-off of PayPal on July 18: eBay shareholders received PayPal shares, and eBay is now a pure online marketplace again.
why: In the game the PayPal shares are folded into the eBay price, so the spin-off shows no drop. On its own eBay grew slowly for years.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EBay (read 2026-10-03); folding of the spin-off per data/src/universe.ts note

title: eBay's growth speeds up
what: On July 20 eBay reported second-quarter revenue of $2.2 billion and merchandise volume of $20.9 billion, raised its forecast for the year and added $2.5 billion to its share buyback. Chief executive Devin Wenig said growth was accelerating; StubHub's sales rose 40%.
why: A rare upturn for the post-PayPal eBay; the shares rose 33% in July 2016.

title: eBay replaces PayPal with Adyen
what: On January 31 eBay announced that it will replace PayPal as its main payment processor with the Dutch company Adyen, lowering its costs and giving it more control over payments.
why: eBay takes back the payments business it had spun off with PayPal.

title: eBay pays its first dividend
what: On January 29 eBay announced its first-ever dividend, 14 cents a share each quarter from March, and $4 billion more for share buybacks, planning to return about $7 billion to shareholders over two years. It has 179 million active buyers.
why: Under pressure from activist investors, eBay becomes a cash-return stock; +20% in January 2019.

title: eBay sells StubHub for $4 billion
what: eBay agreed to sell StubHub, its ticket resale marketplace, to Viagogo for $4.05 billion in cash. Chief executive Devin Wenig left in September under pressure from the activist fund Elliott.
why: eBay sells assets and shrinks back to its core marketplace.

title: Locked-down shoppers turn to eBay
what: On April 29 eBay reported first-quarter revenue of $2.4 billion, 174 million active buyers and gave a business update on Covid-19, which is sending shoppers online. Jamie Iannone has just become chief executive.
why: A pandemic winner: +33% in April 2020 and more than 50% higher by mid-year.

title: eBay sells its classifieds business
what: eBay agreed to sell its classified-ads business, including Germany's Kleinanzeigen, to Adevinta for $2.5 billion in cash and 540 million Adevinta shares.
why: The last big disposal; what remains is the marketplace.

title: eBay sells its Korean business
what: eBay sold its South Korean business to the retailer Emart for $3 billion.
why: Part of the slimming down to the core marketplace and cash returns.

title: eBay buys TCGplayer
what: eBay bought TCGplayer, a marketplace for collectible card games, for about $295 million.
why: Part of eBay's focus on collectibles.

title: eBay cuts 9% of its staff
what: eBay announced it will lay off about 9% of its workforce after hiring outpaced the growth of the business.
why: Cost discipline under Iannone; the shares began a two-year rise.

title: eBay beats expectations
what: On July 30 eBay reported second-quarter revenue of $2.7 billion, up 6%, and merchandise volume of $19.5 billion, up 6%, results the chief executive said exceeded expectations 'across the board'. It is testing an AI shopping agent.
why: The shares rose 23% in July 2025 to their highest level in years.

title: eBay rejects a $56 billion bid from GameStop
what: On May 3 the video game retailer GameStop, which holds about 5% of eBay, proposed to buy eBay for about $56 billion in cash and shares. eBay rejected it as 'neither credible nor attractive'.
why: A sign of how far eBay's value has recovered; the shares stood near record highs.
